newsitem.title: IRAQ: Turkish troops spread hunt for rebels in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Turkish troops spread hunt for rebels in Iraq.

text.p: Turkish troops backed by air power spread their search for Kurdish rebels in the mountainous regions of northern Iraq on Monday on the sixth day of an military operation that has drawn international criticism.

Cobra helicopters and F-4 jets bombed a Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebel camp at Zap near the border with Iran. State-run Anatolian news agency said the camp had been destroyed and some of the rebels were trying to flee across the border.
Ankara has appealed to Tehran to stop the rebels escaping into Iran and finding logistical support there.
In a separate assault, Turkish tanks have moved northeast from the Iraqi town of Dohuk towards Amediye, south of the Turkish border.

Sources close to the rebels said they have shot down three army helicopters since the operation began early last Wednesday. The Turkish army says it lost one helicopter to a "technical fault," killing both pilots.
Communications with the region were blocked, making independent confirmation of the reports impossible.

PKK guerrillas, under heavy assault from troops in the Iraqi border areas, launched hit-and-run attacks in southeast Turkey, witnesses told Reuters correspondent Osman Senkul in the Turkish town of Cizre.
Rebels set up a roadblock on a main road to the northern Iraqi border overnight and set fire to two petrol tankers.
The rebels fled from the scene in Nusaybin on the border with Syria after making a speech in support of their cause and then opening fire on the trucks, they said.
In a separate incident, the rebels launched a rocket attack on the town of Derik in nearby Mardin province, Anatolian said. It said the assault caused little damage.
The Iraq operation has drawn criticism from Western capitals and the United Nations, who have urged Ankara to withdraw the troops and expressed concern for the safety of civilians.
The newspaper of Iraq's ruling Baath party complained on Monday about the Turkish military presence, saying Ankara should reconsider its policy.

"Campaigns of condemnation and denunciation, albeit significant, are not enough. What is needed is that these campaigns turn into an organised international move to pressure Turkey to withdraw its troops," al-Thawra said in a commentary.
Iraq's U.N. coordinator in Baghdad has expressed concern at the incursion, saying it might block implementation of Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the world body.

On Monday, military officials at the Turkish Habur border crossing into northern Iraq continued to enforce a ban on journalists entering the region. Access was limited to Iraqi passport holders and those involved in cross-border oil trade.

Four attack helicopters and another four carrying supplies flew across the border towards the Batufa region on Monday. Around 20 military trucks ferried supplies through Habur to Iraq, witnesses said.
Military sources say the rebel death toll in northern Iraq stood at over 1,000, with around 150 guerrillas captured. They put the number of soldiers killed at 14.

Pro-Kurdish MED-TV said more than 30 Turkish soldiers had been killed in fighting with the rebels. It made no mention of PKK casualties in northern Iraq, but said one guerrilla had been killed in clashes with soldiers in eastern Turkey, in which 15 troops died.

Ankara says the operation was launched in response to a call from the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), which controls much of northern Iraq, and was aimed at protecting civilians from a possible "massacre" by the PKK.
A rival Iraqi Kurdish group is in control further south in the region, set up as an autonomous Kurdish zone by the West following the 1991 Gulf War.
